name: Burnt matchstick mascara

lead:
Before commercial mascara was widespread, people darkened lashes at home with soot-like materials. Popular histories of early-1900s makeup describe burnt matches among these, alongside burnt cork, lampblack and coal dust, often mixed with petroleum jelly.
The payoff was darker, more defined lashes and eyes that looked larger. Maybelline's mail-order Lash-Brow-Ine, launched in the 1910s, is the commercial successor often cited in the story.

paras: The popular descriptions involve charring a match tip and applying the soot to the lashes, sometimes with a little grease. No instructions are given here.
Homemade soot is not a tested cosmetic ingredient, and the eye area is sensitive; the main concerns are irritation and contamination.

chain: Soot from a charred match or similar material is applied to lashes
Lashes appear darker and more defined
angle.text: Soot darkens lashes at once, as later cake and cream mascaras did. It was a stopgap before commercial products became widely available.

lead: Burnt matchstick mascara refers to the practice, described in popular histories of early 20th-century beauty, of darkening eyelashes with the soot from a burnt match. Contemporary-era histories more commonly list homemade lash blends of lampblack, coal dust, burnt cork, ash or elderberry juice. [1]

The aim was the same as modern mascara: lashes that look darker and denser, framing the eyes. The commercial turn came in the 1910s: Benjamin Ansehl started Lashbrow Laboratories in 1912, and T. L. Williams sold Lash-Brow-Ine by mail order from about 1915-1917, later developing Maybelline. [2] A widely told origin story says Williams saw his sister Mabel darken her lashes with burnt cork and petroleum jelly, which the source presents as a commonly told tale rather than documented fact. [2]
No studies have examined burnt-match lash darkening.
infobox: Burnt match, burnt cork, lampblack, coal dust

paras: Lisa Eldridge's history lists lampblack made from a candle flame, coal dust, burnt cork and ash as homemade lash darkeners used before commercial mascara. [1] Burnt matches are mentioned in popular histories as part of this tradition.

Ansehl's Lashbrow Laboratories (1912) sold a petrolatum, beeswax and lampblack or willow charcoal product. [2] Williams obtained a petrolatum-based cream and sold it as Lash-Brow-Ine, registering the trademark in 1917; sales topped $100,000 in 1920, and a court ruled the trademark invalid. [2] Maybelline appeared in 1917 as a cake mascara, and a liquid form in 1925. [2]
No specific injuries from this practice have been reported. Soot and burnt household materials are not formulated or tested for eye use.

timeline.event: Lashbrow Laboratories founded in St. Louis. [2]
